title: Inside the Ramparts: Copenhagen, Berlin, and the Attack Upon Christendom
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Nytorv 2, the seventh child
stops.date_confidence: attested; birth date and house from sorenkierkegaard.org, corroborated by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Coordinate corrected: Wikipedia's article on Nytorv puts the square at 55.6775, 12.5731, while the pool's 12.5701 fell on Gammeltorv, some 190 m west. Note a gap: the dedicated encyclopedia articles on Nytorv and on the Church of Our Lady do not mention Kierkegaard at all, and no commemorative marker at either site turned up in reachable sources. That is a gap in the record, not proof no marker exists.
stops.campa: The wool merchant Michael Pedersen Kierkegaard, who came to Copenhagen off the Jutland heath as a poor boy and made a fortune in cloth, has a seventh child in the house on Nytorv, across the square from the courthouse. The father is fifty-six and devout to the point of gloom. The mother, Ane Sørensdatter Lund, was the household servant he married after his first wife died. Of the seven children born in this house, five will be dead before the father is; the two left standing will be Peter Christian and this one. The boy is small, crooked in the back, and quick with his tongue.
suggested_refs: The Kierkegaard house at Nytorv 2, opposite the Copenhagen courthouse

stops.name: Helligåndskirken, the baptism
stops.date_confidence: attested (sorenkierkegaard.org). Coordinate corrected to the church itself, 55.6790, 12.5769, per Wikipedia's article on the Church of the Holy Ghost; the pool's figure landed on Strøget about 150 m west.
stops.campa: Four weeks old, he is carried up to the Church of the Holy Ghost and christened Søren Aabye, the second name out of his mother's family. The church is a medieval Latin foundation turned Lutheran, one of a handful of parishes inside the ramparts. The whole of his religious geography will fit inside a twenty-minute walk: this church, the cathedral where he is confirmed and buried from, the university across the square from the cathedral. He is baptized into the Danish state church without anybody asking him. The register gives the date as the third of June.
suggested_refs: Helligåndskirken, Copenhagen, parish church of the baptism
sources: Wikipedia, 'Church of the Holy Ghost, Copenhagen'

stops.name: Borgerdydskolen, the fork
stops.date_confidence: Attendance from 1821 is attested (sorenkierkegaard.org); day and month defaulted to January, the pool gives only the year. The nickname Gaffelen, the fork, is [R]: it comes from schoolfellows' memoirs collected decades later in Kirmmse's Encounters with Kierkegaard, not from any contemporary document.
stops.campa: He is sent to the School of Civic Virtue in Klareboderne, dressed by his father in old-fashioned clothes that make him a mark the day he walks in. He is slight, badly built, and cannot fight. What he has instead is a tongue. Schoolfellows remembering him half a century later call him the fork, because he found the tender place in an opponent and went into it. He is good at Latin and better at argument, and he is not liked. In the evenings his father examines him at the table on what the day taught him.
suggested_refs: Bruce H. Kirmmse, ed., Encounters with Kierkegaard, for the schoolfellows' recollections

stops.name: Vor Frue Kirke, the confirmation
stops.date_confidence: attested (sorenkierkegaard.org). Coordinate corrected to 55.67944, 12.57278 per Wikipedia's article on the Church of Our Lady; the pool carried a figure about 95 m south and repeated it identically at four separate stops.
stops.campa: At not quite fifteen he is confirmed in the cathedral by Bishop Jacob Peter Mynster, his father's pastor and the most respected churchman in Denmark, a man the household treats as an authority sitting just under God. The boy takes the rite as it comes and goes home to dinner. Twenty-six years from now, at this altar, a sentence spoken over Mynster's coffin will set off the loudest quarrel of Kierkegaard's life. For now Mynster preaches order, moderation, and a Christianity a decent Copenhagen family can live inside without discomfort.
suggested_refs: Vor Frue Kirke, Copenhagen, church of the confirmation, the 1854 funeral of Mynster, and Kierkegaard's own funeral

stops.name: Frue Plads, matriculation and the examinations
stops.date_confidence: attested (sorenkierkegaard.org). Correction to the pool, which folded two examinations into one entry: sorenkierkegaard.org separates them, first examination 25 April 1831 magna cum laude in languages and history, second examination 27 October 1831 summa cum laude in philosophy. Both are given here; the pool's single line calling the October exam one in classics, mathematics and philosophy is wrong.
stops.campa: He matriculates in theology, the route his father expects, and clears the preliminary work in a year: first examination in April 1831 in languages and history, second in October in philosophy, both with the highest marks the faculty gives. Then he stops. Ten years pass between this and the theological degree, ten years of borrowed money, cigars, the theatre, and reading that has nothing to do with any parish. He stays enrolled and does not study. The father pays the bills and says little about them.
suggested_refs: The University of Copenhagen at Frue Plads, facing the cathedral

stops.name: Nytorv 2, the mother
stops.date_confidence: attested (sorenkierkegaard.org). The absence of the mother from the journals is a documented feature of the surviving papers and is stated here as such, not as an inference about what she meant to him.
stops.campa: Ane Sørensdatter Lund dies in the house, and her son writes nothing about her. She is almost absent from the journals he has just started keeping: no scene, no grief on the page, not a sentence of the kind he spends on the weather and on strangers in the street. Whether that silence is indifference, or something he could not get onto a page, the papers do not say. Of the seven children she bore here, two are left. The father, seventy-eight and convinced a curse is working itself out through the family, expects to bury the rest of them and outlive them all.
suggested_refs: Søren Kierkegaards Skrifter, the journals of 1834, for the silence on the mother's death

stops.name: Nytorv 2, the great earthquake
stops.date_confidence: [R] as to date and content. sorenkierkegaard.org puts the great earthquake in 1835 and states the content directly, the discovery of the father's curse on God; the journal entry itself carries no date, and scholars have redated the episode as late as 1838 and disagree over how literally to read it. What is contested is the dating and the reading, not that the entry exists. The pool's claim that the content was never specified overstates the mystery. Day and month defaulted to order the segment. The quoted entry is given at sorenkierkegaard.org as II A 805 with no translator named; cross-check against SKS or the Hong Journals before quoting further.
stops.campa: Something the father says, or something the son finds out, breaks the household's account of itself. The journal calls it the great earthquake and dates nothing. What is recorded is a discovery about Michael Pedersen Kierkegaard: a boy on the Jutland heath, hungry, standing on a hill and cursing God, and in the wider tradition a transgression afterward against the servant who became his second wife. The son reads the family's dead children backward from it, as a sentence being served. He is twenty-two. He stops coming home.
stops.quote: It was then the great earthquake occurred, the terrible upheaval which suddenly pressed on me a new infallible law for the interpretation of all phenomena.
stops.quote_source: Journals, entry II A 805, quoted at sorenkierkegaard.org; no translator named on the page consulted
suggested_refs: Søren Kierkegaards Skrifter, journal entry II A 805, and the scholarly dispute over its dating

stops.name: Gilbjerg Hoved, the idea
stops.date_confidence: The 1835 Gilleleje stay is attested (sorenkierkegaard.org); the precise spot of composition is [R], identified by tradition with the clifftop at Gilbjerg Hoved, where a memorial stone carries the line. Coordinate corrected to 56.1290, 12.2869, the northernmost point of Zealand per the Danish Wikipedia article on Gilbjerg Hoved; the pool's figure sat about 700 m offshore in the Kattegat. Month set to August within the summer stay.
stops.campa: Sent north to recover, he walks the clay cliffs at the top of Zealand where the land stops and the Kattegat starts, and writes the sentence that will later be cut into a stone at this spot: what he needs is a truth that is true for him, the idea for which he is willing to live and die. He is not writing philosophy yet. He is a theology student on holiday, in debt, quietly refusing the career his father bought him, working out on a cliff path what he is for. The memorial stone on the clifftop carries the line.
stops.quote: Hvad er sandhed andet end en leven for en idé
stops.quote_source: Inscription on the Kierkegaard memorial stone at Gilbjerg Hoved, Gilleleje, taken from the journal of the 1835 stay
suggested_refs: The Kierkegaard memorial stone on the clifftop at Gilbjerg Hoved, above Gilleleje

stops.name: Kongens Nytorv, the theatre
stops.date_confidence: [R] as a recurring habit rather than a dated visit; the date orders the segment. Coordinate corrected to roughly 55.6797, 12.5854 on Kongens Nytorv. Two corrections to the pool: sorenkierkegaard.org's biography page does not in fact mention Fru Heiberg or the Royal Theatre, so that attribution is dropped, and the Heiberg connection rests instead on Wikipedia's article on Johanne Luise Heiberg, which dates 'The Crisis and a Crisis in the Life of an Actress' to 1847 and does not confirm the Juliet framing. Also an anachronism worth naming: the building on the square today is Dahlerup's Old Stage of 1872-74, put up nearly two decades after his death.
stops.campa: He goes to the Royal Theatre the way other men go to church, and to Mozart's Don Giovanni over and over, until the opera turns into an argument he can make in prose about desire with no object but itself. He follows the actress Johanne Luise Heiberg closely enough to write a study of her second career on the stage. The house he sits in is not the one standing on the square now; that goes up in the 1870s, long after he is dead. His is the older theatre on the same square, and he sits in the cheap seats.
stops.quote: When I grew older and opened my eyes and contemplated the real world, I had to laugh, and have not ceased laughing, ever since.
stops.quote_source: Either/Or, 'Diapsalmata', trans. Lee M. Hollander, Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard (1923)
suggested_refs: Kierkegaard, 'The Crisis and a Crisis in the Life of an Actress' (1847), on Johanne Luise Heiberg

stops.name: Frederiksberg, the Rørdam house
stops.date_confidence: The meeting is attested (Wikipedia, 'Regine Olsen'; sorenkierkegaard.org narrows it to 8-12 May 1837), and 10 May is set within that window. Correction to the pool, which called Regine eighteen: she was born 23 January 1822 and was fifteen. The coordinate is [R], an approximate placement, and a poor one: 55.6786, 12.5309 sits at the northeastern edge of the district, well north of Frederiksberg proper at about 55.667, 12.533. The Rørdam house itself is not identifiable from any reachable source.
stops.campa: Visiting the widow Catrine Rørdam's household out in Frederiksberg, he meets Regine Olsen, a state councillor's daughter of fifteen. He is twenty-four, in debt, living apart from his father, and publishing nothing. Then nothing happens for three years. He does not court her, does not write to her, and by his own later account settles the whole matter in that room and afterward simply waits. The house cannot be identified from anything now reachable; only the district is certain.
suggested_refs: Joakim Garff, Kierkegaard's Muse, on Regine Olsen's own account of the meeting

stops.name: Reitzel's, From the Papers of One Still Living
stops.date_confidence: The 1838 book is attested in the Stanford Encyclopedia's publication list and at sorenkierkegaard.org; day and month are defaulted, the pool gives only the year. The Andersen-critique framing was itself flagged in the pool as resting on the dossier rather than on a page fetched during verification: it is standard in the bibliographies but has not been checked here against the text. That the two men avoided each other afterward is [R], biographical tradition. Reitzel's shop address is [R], a reconstructed placement in the booksellers' quarter near the university.
stops.campa: His first book is a small hostile review of Hans Christian Andersen's novel Only a Fiddler, published under a title meaning, roughly, papers left behind by a man not yet dead. The argument is that Andersen has no view of life and so cannot make a character who has one, that he writes genius as a thing too delicate to survive contact with the world. Andersen is famous, thin-skinned, and lives in the same small city. He reads it. The two of them keep out of each other's way for twenty years.
suggested_refs: Kierkegaard, Af en endnu Levendes Papirer (1838), on Andersen's Kun en Spillemand

stops.name: Nytorv 2, the father
stops.date_confidence: attested (sorenkierkegaard.org), which gives the death as 9 August 1838 and the burial in the family plot at Assistens as 14 August 1838; the five-day interval is ordinary and not a contradiction. The reading of the death as a sacrifice made for him is Kierkegaard's own, recorded in the journals.
stops.campa: Michael Pedersen Kierkegaard dies in the house at eighty-two, and the son who had been refusing him for years decides at once that the death was a sacrifice made on his behalf: the old man went so that the young one might still become something. He is buried on the fourteenth in the family plot at Assistens, out in Nørrebro. The estate leaves Søren free of any need to earn money for the rest of his life. Within two years he sits the theological examination he had been avoiding since 1831.
suggested_refs: The Kierkegaard family plot at Assistens Kirkegård, Nørrebro

stops.name: Sædding Sogn, the father's heath
stops.date_confidence: The journey and its dates, 19 July to 6 August 1840, are attested at sorenkierkegaard.org, which names no village. Major correction to the pool, which used Sædding the Esbjerg suburb at 55.49, 8.42, a modern parish with no Kierkegaard connection, some sixty kilometres off. The family's parish is Sædding Sogn in Bølling Herred, old Ringkøbing Amt, today Ringkøbing-Skjern Kommune, at about 56.03, 8.55. Which stretch of heath he actually walked is [R]; that he was looking for the site of the curse is inference from the journals.
stops.campa: Sixteen days after passing the theological examination he takes the long ride into west Jutland, to the parish his father came from, and walks the heath where Michael Pedersen herded sheep before an uncle fetched him to Copenhagen. He is looking for the hill of the curse. He finds relatives who are farmers, sees the church his father's people sat in, and sleeps in poor rooms. Whether he found the hill, or knew it when he saw it, the journals do not record. He turns east again in the first week of August.
suggested_refs: Sædding Sogn, Bølling Herred, the Kierkegaard family's parish on the west Jutland heath

stops.name: Børsgade, the proposal
stops.date_confidence: attested (sorenkierkegaard.org; Wikipedia, 'Regine Olsen'): proposal 8 September 1840, formal engagement entered 10 September 1840. The street is attested as Børsgade near Knippelsbro; the house number is not found in any reachable source, so the coordinate is [R] at street level.
stops.campa: He walks to the Olsen house near Knippelsbro, finds Regine alone, and asks her father for her the same evening. Terkild Olsen says yes. The formal engagement is entered two days later. She is eighteen and has been half promised already to her former tutor, Johan Frederik Schlegel. Almost immediately Kierkegaard writes in the journal that he has made a mistake, that the engagement cannot hold, that he is too melancholy to be a husband to anybody. Regine is told none of it until the following August.
suggested_refs: The Olsen family house in Børsgade, near Knippelsbro, Copenhagen

stops.name: Holmens Kirke, the trial sermon
stops.date_confidence: attested (sorenkierkegaard.org), which also records a sermon at Trinitatis Church on 24 February 1844. How many times in total he preached is not established by any source consulted.
stops.campa: To finish the pastoral requirements he preaches a trial sermon at Holmens Church, the navy's parish, in front of examiners. He passes. He preaches again at Trinitatis in February 1844 and a handful of times after, and never once applies for a living. The whole apparatus of ordination now stands open to him and he walks past it, leaving it there unused for the next fifteen years while he writes books about what Christianity demands. He preaches perhaps a dozen times in his life.
suggested_refs: Holmens Kirke, Copenhagen, the navy's parish church

stops.name: Børsgade, the ring returned
stops.date_confidence: attested (sorenkierkegaard.org; Wikipedia, 'Regine Olsen'). The deliberate cultivation of a seducer's appearance is his own account in the journals, repeated across the standard biographies; it is his testimony about his own motives, not an independent record.
stops.campa: He sends back the engagement ring with a letter. Regine refuses to accept the break. Her father comes to him and asks him not to do it, says it will be the death of her, and he agrees to hold on a while longer. The journal records the strategy of the next two months while it is running: he sets about making himself impossible on purpose, playing the cold man, showing up at the theatre where she will see him, so the fault will lie visibly with him and the town will say she was well rid of him.
suggested_refs: Kierkegaard's letters to Regine Olsen, August to October 1841

stops.name: Frue Plads, On the Concept of Irony
stops.date_confidence: attested (sorenkierkegaard.org; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy). The special dispensation to write and defend in Danish rather than Latin is standard in the biographies and is [R] here; it was not re-verified against a fetched source.
stops.campa: He defends the dissertation in public and takes the magister degree, two weeks before he ends the engagement. The subject is Socrates: irony not as a trick of speech but as a way of standing toward a whole age, the man who says less than he knows and lets the questioning do the work on other people. The faculty finds it long and impertinent. Against Hegel, who treats irony as a stage thought passes through on its way somewhere better, Kierkegaard treats it as a position a living person can actually occupy.
suggested_refs: Om Begrebet Ironi med stadigt Hensyn til Socrates (1841), defended at the University of Copenhagen

stops.name: Børsgade, the engagement broken
stops.date_confidence: attested (sorenkierkegaard.org; Wikipedia, 'Regine Olsen'). The dialogue of the last meeting comes from Kierkegaard's journals and from Regine's recollections given decades afterward, not from any contemporary third-party record.
stops.campa: The last meeting. She asks whether he will never marry, and he answers that in ten years, when he has worn himself out, he will need a young girl to make him young again. He writes afterward that he said it to make her hate him, and that he went home and cried the night through. The engagement is finished. Two weeks later he is on a ship to Berlin. Regine's family and half of Copenhagen settle on the verdict that he is a scoundrel, which is the verdict he built.
stops.quote: he clearly recognizes the impossibility, and in the same moment he believes the absurd; for if he imagined he had faith, without at the same time recognizing... that his love is impossible, he would be merely deceiving himself
stops.quote_source: Fear and Trembling, trans. Lee M. Hollander, Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard (1923)
suggested_refs: Joakim Garff, Kierkegaard's Muse, for Regine Schlegel's later account of the break

stops.name: Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität, Schelling and the word actuality
stops.date_confidence: attested: the 25 October 1841 departure and the stay to March 1842 are at sorenkierkegaard.org, and the Schelling attendance is confirmed independently by the Stanford Encyclopedia. The 15 November date of the inaugural lecture is inherited from schelling.journey.json, and the coordinate is the canonical Berlin pin used byte-identically by the schelling, hegel, bakunin and humboldt files. The documented co-attendance of Bakunin, Engels, Burckhardt and Humboldt is co-presence at one lecture course only, with no meeting recorded, so none of them is named in the campa.
stops.campa: Two weeks out of Copenhagen he takes a seat in the crowded aula for Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling's inaugural lecture on the philosophy of revelation, the course Berlin has fetched the old man out of retirement to give against Hegel's system. Kierkegaard writes that the child of thought leaped for joy within him when Schelling said the word actuality. He fills a notebook. He is twenty-eight, three weeks clear of an engagement he wrecked on purpose, and he has come the length of the Baltic to hear a man of sixty-six say that thought and being are not the same thing.
stops.quote: The embryonic child of thought leapt for joy within me... when he mentioned the word actuality
stops.quote_source: Kierkegaard's journal on Schelling's Berlin lectures, quoted at sorenkierkegaard.org/schellings-lecture-notes.html
suggested_refs: Kierkegaard's Berlin notebook on Schelling's Philosophie der Offenbarung, 1841-42, alongside the notes kept in the same hall by Engels and Burckhardt
sources: schelling.journey.json (canonical Berlin pin and lecture date)

stops.name: Gendarmenmarkt, the winter lodging
stops.date_confidence: The Gendarmenmarkt lodging is [R]: asserted in the dossier and confirmed by no source fetched during verification. The souring on Schelling by February 1842 is attested in the journals and carried in schelling.journey.json; the return to Copenhagen on 6 March 1842 is attested at sorenkierkegaard.org. Day and month defaulted to order the segment.
stops.campa: He lodges near the Gendarmenmarkt, takes German lessons, goes to the theatre and to the opera, and writes. By February the Schelling lectures have gone sour on him; the talk of potencies is insufferable nonsense, he says, and he stops attending altogether. What he does instead, in rented rooms in a foreign city with nobody in it who knows his name, is draft a two-volume book by a man who does not exist. He is back in Copenhagen on the sixth of March 1842 with most of Either/Or in his luggage.
suggested_refs: The Gendarmenmarkt quarter of Berlin, traditional site of Kierkegaard's 1841-42 lodging

stops.name: Reitzel's, Either/Or
stops.date_confidence: attested (sorenkierkegaard.org; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy). Reitzel's shop address is [R], a reconstructed placement in the booksellers' quarter near the university, used for all the publication stops in this file.
stops.campa: C. A. Reitzel publishes two volumes edited by one Victor Eremita, who explains that he found the papers in the secret drawer of a second-hand writing desk: an aesthete's fragments and seduction diary in the first, a married judge's long letters on choosing oneself in the second, no author's name anywhere in either. Copenhagen reads it as a scandal and a puzzle and reads the seducer as a confession about Regine. It sells out. Kierkegaard walks the streets denying he wrote it, and goes on denying it, book after book under invented names, for the next four years.
stops.quote: In addition to my numerous other acquaintances I have still one more intimate friend my melancholy.
stops.quote_source: Either/Or, 'Diapsalmata', trans. Lee M. Hollander, Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard (1923)
suggested_refs: Enten-Eller, published by C. A. Reitzel, Copenhagen, 20 February 1843

stops.name: Vor Frue Kirke, the encounter
stops.date_confidence: attested (sorenkierkegaard.org). Coordinate corrected as at the confirmation stop. That he arranged his walking routes so as to pass her is [R], drawn from the journals' own register of these sightings rather than from any statement of intent.
stops.campa: Two months after Either/Or he sees Regine at the cathedral, or she sees him, and he writes it down. He keeps a private register of these encounters for years: times, places, the nod at Easter, whether she looked, what he did with his face, on routes he arranges so as to pass her. She will be engaged again before long, to Schlegel, her old tutor. The books Copenhagen is reading as an attack on her are being written a few hundred metres from where she lives.
suggested_refs: The journals of 1843-1849, for Kierkegaard's running record of the Regine sightings

stops.name: Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität, the returning journeys
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction inside the pool, resolved here and flagged: the chronology lens called the second trip 'summer 1843', the geography lens 'May 1843'. sorenkierkegaard.org gives a second trip in 1843 returning at the end of June, so May to end of June 1843 is the reading used. The third trip, 13-24 May 1845, is attested at sorenkierkegaard.org. Both are folded into one stop. Coordinate inherited from the canonical Berlin pin. The quotation is a literal rendering of the Danish of Pap. IV A 164 (= JJ:167); the familiar English one-liner 'Life can only be understood backwards, but it must be lived forwards' is a popular condensation circulating in several inconsistent forms with no named translator, and is not used.
stops.campa: He goes back to Berlin in May 1843 and stays until the end of June, then again for eleven days in May 1845: the same route, the same city, on purpose, to find out whether a thing can be had a second time. The Danish word he uses is Gjentagelsen, repetition, which is not memory running backward but the same thing got forward, again. Whether he is also testing whether Regine could be had back is the reading the journals invite and never state. The book he writes out of the experiment reports that it fails.
stops.quote: It is quite true what philosophy says, that life must be understood backwards. But then one forgets the other proposition, that it must be lived forwards.
stops.quote_source: Journals, 1843, Pap. IV A 164 (= JJ:167); literal rendering of the Danish, not a named published translation
suggested_refs: Gjentagelsen (1843), written out of the second Berlin journey

stops.name: Reitzel's, Fear and Trembling and Repetition
stops.date_confidence: attested (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; sorenkierkegaard.org): both pseudonymous books and the Three Upbuilding Discourses appeared on 16 October 1843. Reitzel coordinate [R] as above. The reading of Abraham as a displaced Regine is Kierkegaard's own in the journals and is the standard biographical reading; it is an interpretation, not a documented statement of intent inside the book.
stops.campa: In one day two books appear by two men who do not exist, Johannes de silentio and Constantin Constantius, together with three upbuilding discourses signed with his own name. One of them puts Abraham on the three days' ride to Moriah and refuses to let the reader off the hook: if the man is the father of faith then the ethical was suspended for him, and if it was not suspended, he was riding out to murder a child. Kierkegaard, who has just given up the girl he wanted, writes the knight of faith as the one who gets Isaac back.
stops.quote: Not only in the world of commerce but also in the world of ideas our age has arranged a regular clearance-sale.
stops.quote_source: Fear and Trembling, Preface, trans. Lee M. Hollander, Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard (1923)
suggested_refs: Frygt og Bæven and Gjentagelsen, both published 16 October 1843

stops.name: Reitzel's, Fragments and Anxiety
stops.date_confidence: attested, and a correction to the pool, which gave a bare 1844 and implied joint publication. sorenkierkegaard.org dates Philosophical Fragments to 13 June 1844 and The Concept of Anxiety to 17 June 1844: four days apart, not together. Reitzel coordinate [R].
stops.campa: Four days apart, two more pseudonyms. Johannes Climacus asks whether an eternal consciousness can have a historical point of departure, and answers with the paradox: the god in time, which reason cannot think and can only take offence at. Vigilius Haufniensis works the same question from the other side and calls anxiety the dizziness of freedom, the state of a creature looking down at what it could do. Neither book carries his name. Both are on the same shop counter in the same week of June.
suggested_refs: Philosophiske Smuler (13 June 1844) and Begrebet Angest (17 June 1844)

stops.name: Frederiksberg Have, the walking method
stops.date_confidence: [R] as a recurring practice rather than a dated visit; the date orders the segment. The walking method is attested in general terms, including in the Stanford Encyclopedia's account of how the Corsair affair put an end to it, but Frederiksberg Have specifically could not be confirmed against the other Copenhagen routes he used. The population figure is the standard one for Copenhagen inside the ramparts in the 1840s and was not verified against a census in this pass.
stops.campa: The working day is a walk. He writes standing at a high desk through the morning, then goes out into the streets and the gardens and talks to whoever is there, servants, tradesmen, students, children, keeping the conversation going until something in it turns over, and then goes home fast and writes it down while it is still hot. People set their clocks by him. Copenhagen inside the ramparts is a town of something over a hundred thousand people, and he knows it on foot.
stops.quote: Of all ridiculous things the most ridiculous seems to me, to be busy to be a man who is brisk about his food and his work.
stops.quote_source: Either/Or, 'Diapsalmata', trans. Lee M. Hollander, Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard (1923)
suggested_refs: Frederiksberg Have and the streets inside the Copenhagen ramparts, the ground of the daily walks

stops.name: Reitzel's, Stages on Life's Way
stops.date_confidence: The 30 April 1845 date comes from the standard Kierkegaard bibliography as relayed in the pool and was not re-verified against a page fetched in this pass; treat it as [A] in the bibliographies, unchecked here. Reitzel coordinate [R]. The quoted line is a pseudonym's speech at a fictional banquet and is flagged as such in the quote source.
stops.campa: A third book in layers, assembled by a bookbinder called Hilarius who insists he only had the papers bound. It opens with five men at a banquet talking about women, moves to a judge's defence of marriage, and closes with the diary of a man who broke off an engagement and cannot stop going back over it, entry by entry, a year on. The distance between the author and his material has become a public joke in Copenhagen. The critic P. L. Møller is about to put the joke into print.
stops.quote: Woman is understood correctly only when placed in the category of 'the joke.'
stops.quote_source: Stages on Life's Way, 'In Vino Veritas', trans. Lee M. Hollander, Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard (1923); spoken by the pseudonym Constantin Constantius, not by Kierkegaard in his own name
suggested_refs: Stadier paa Livets Vei (1845), edited by the pseudonymous Hilarius Bogbinder

stops.name: Fædrelandet, the traveling esthetician
stops.date_confidence: attested, and a correction to the pool, which put Møller's review on 27 December. Wikipedia's article on Kierkegaard dates Møller's piece in Gæa to 22 December 1845; sorenkierkegaard.org dates Kierkegaard's reply in Fædrelandet to 27 December 1845. The newspaper's office address is [R], a reconstructed placement in central Copenhagen.
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of December the critic Peder Ludvig Møller publishes a piece on Stages in the yearbook Gæa, treating the author as a man who tortured a woman for literary material. Five days later Kierkegaard answers in Fædrelandet under the name Frater Taciturnus and does two things at once. He takes Møller apart, and he names him as a secret contributor to Corsaren, the anonymous satirical weekly that everybody in Copenhagen reads and nobody admits to reading. Then he asks Corsaren, in print, to abuse him.
suggested_refs: 'The Activity of a Traveling Esthetician', Fædrelandet, 27 December 1845

stops.name: Reitzel's, A Literary Review
stops.date_confidence: The book is attested for 1846 in the Stanford Encyclopedia's publication list; day and month are defaulted because the pool gives only the year, so its position relative to the Corsair caricatures beginning on 2 January 1846 is approximate and should not be read as sequence. Reitzel coordinate [R].
stops.campa: Under cover of reviewing a novel by Thomasine Gyllembourg he writes the diagnosis of the age: a time without passion, which neither acts nor revolts but talks, in which a phantom called the public is manufactured by the press and holds opinions that no actual person holds. Everybody is informed and nobody is committed. He is writing in the season the press turns and comes for him. Levelling is his word for it, the quiet abolition of the individual by the abstraction called everybody.
stops.quote: Let others complain that the times are wicked. I complain that they are paltry; for they are without passion.
stops.quote_source: Either/Or, 'Diapsalmata', trans. Lee M. Hollander, Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard (1923)
suggested_refs: En literair Anmeldelse (1846), on Thomasine Gyllembourg's To Tidsaldre

stops.name: Corsaren, the caricatures
stops.date_confidence: The campaign and its start on 2 January 1846 are attested (sorenkierkegaard.org), and Goldschmidt's editorship of Corsaren from its founding in 1840 until he sold it in 1846 is confirmed by Wikipedia. The office address is [R], a reconstructed placement in central Copenhagen; the pool tagged this stop attested while its own note conceded the placement was a reconstruction, and the tag is corrected here.
stops.campa: Corsaren, edited by Meïr Aron Goldschmidt, obliges him. From the second of January the paper runs him week after week: the bent back, the uneven trouser legs, the thin shanks, the umbrella, the walk, the girl he jilted. The drawings work. Schoolboys shout after him in the street, the trouser joke becomes a tailor's joke, and the man who conducted his entire working life on the pavement can no longer cross his own town without a crowd forming behind him. He gives up the daily walks.
stops.quote: Behold, therefore would I rather be a swineherd on Amager, and be understood by the swine than a poet, and misunderstood by men.
stops.quote_source: Either/Or, 'Diapsalmata', trans. Lee M. Hollander, Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard (1923)
suggested_refs: The Corsaren caricatures of Kierkegaard, January to July 1846

stops.name: Reitzel's, Concluding Unscientific Postscript
stops.date_confidence: attested (sorenkierkegaard.org; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy). That he meant this book to end the authorship is his own statement, in the appended declaration and in the journals. Reitzel coordinate [R].
stops.campa: Six hundred pages against the System, published by Johannes Climacus with Kierkegaard named on the title page only as editor, and closed with a signed statement in which he claims the whole pseudonymous authorship as his and asks that not one word of it be quoted as his own opinion. Truth is subjectivity. An existing individual cannot take up the position from which Hegel surveys world history, because he is inside the history and is going to die in it. He means this to be the last book, and says so in print.
suggested_refs: Afsluttende uvidenskabelig Efterskrift (1846) and its appended 'A First and Last Declaration'

stops.name: Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität, the last journey
stops.date_confidence: attested, and a correction to the pool's geography lens, which gave 'May-June 1846' and called this the least certain of the four Berlin datings. sorenkierkegaard.org dates the fourth trip to 2-16 May 1846, agreeing with the pool's own chronology lens; it is as firmly dated as the third. Coordinate inherited from the canonical Berlin pin.
stops.campa: Two weeks in Berlin, the second to the sixteenth of May. It is the fourth time he has been abroad, always to this same city, and it is the last: after this he leaves Denmark for nothing further off than a crossing of the Sound. He has been publicly ridiculed for four months at home and has just published the book that was supposed to close his authorship for good. Instead of stopping he begins the second one, the signed one, on Christian categories.
suggested_refs: The fourth and last Berlin journey, 2-16 May 1846

stops.name: Reitzel's, Works of Love
stops.date_confidence: Attested for 1847 in the Stanford Encyclopedia's publication list; day and month defaulted, the pool gives only the year. Reitzel coordinate [R]. The link drawn here to the Corsair caricatures is the writer's juxtaposition of two attested facts, not a claim the book names them.
stops.campa: Signed with his own name, and the hardest book he writes. He is writing it in a city where he can no longer take a walk without being laughed at by people who have seen his trousers drawn in a weekly paper. Love of the neighbour is not a feeling but a command, and a command can be obeyed toward a person one does not like. Preference is not love at all, he argues: the friend and the beloved are the self doubled and admired. The neighbour is whoever happens to be in front of you.
suggested_refs: Kjerlighedens Gjerninger (1847)

stops.name: Nytorv 2, Regine married
stops.date_confidence: Sources disagree on the day and are not reconciled here. Wikipedia's article on Regine Olsen gives 3 November 1847, at Vor Frelsers Kirke in Christianshavn; sorenkierkegaard.org's chronology gives 9 November 1847; the Danish Wikipedia article on Kierkegaard gives only 1848. November 1847 is the safe statement, and the venue, which no version of the pool's claim mentioned, is added from Wikipedia. The stop sits at Kierkegaard's own house rather than at the church because he was not there. The will and Regine's refusal of the inheritance are attested (Wikipedia, 'Regine Olsen').
stops.campa: Regine Olsen marries Johan Frederik Schlegel at the Church of Our Saviour over in Christianshavn. Kierkegaard is not there. He goes on recording her in the journals for the rest of his life, and the will he draws up leaves everything he owns to her, on the stated ground that an engagement is as binding as a marriage. She will refuse the money, then accept it only as a trustee, to give away to the poor. He sells the house on Nytorv the following year.
suggested_refs: Vor Frelsers Kirke, Christianshavn, where Regine Olsen married Frederik Schlegel in November 1847
Kierkegaard's will, and Regine Schlegel's response to it in probate

stops.name: Reitzel's, The Sickness Unto Death
stops.date_confidence: Attested for 1849 (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; sorenkierkegaard.org); day and month defaulted, the pool gives only the year. Reitzel coordinate [R]. The suggested reference to Adorno's habilitation is a later commentator's engagement, cited here as a reference on Kierkegaard's own stop rather than staged as a scene; see the report for the direction flag.
stops.campa: A new pseudonym, Anti-Climacus, pitched above him rather than below: a Christian of a severity Kierkegaard does not claim for himself. The book defines the self as a relation that relates itself to itself, and defines despair as that relation gone wrong, and then argues that despair is universal and mostly unnoticed, that the man who does not know he is in it is the worst off of all. The sickness unto death is not dying. It is not being able to die.
suggested_refs: Sygdommen til Døden (1849), by Anti-Climacus
Theodor W. Adorno, Kierkegaard: Construction of the Aesthetic (habilitation 1929-31, published 1933), a later study of Kierkegaard's aesthetics
sources: theodor_adorno.journey.json (for the Frankfurt habilitation on Kierkegaard)

stops.name: Nørregade 43, Practice in Christianity
stops.date_confidence: The move to Nørregade 43 on 18 April 1850 is attested (sorenkierkegaard.org); the book is attested for 1850 (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy) without a day in the pool, so the stop takes the date of the move. The coordinate is [R]: historic Nørregade numbering does not map cleanly onto the modern street. Mynster's displeasure at the book is [R], biographical tradition. The quoted journal passage carries no entry number and no translator on the page consulted and needs cross-checking against SKS or the Hong Journals.
stops.campa: He moves to Nørregade in April and publishes in the autumn, again as Anti-Climacus. Christ is not a figure the centuries have safely explained; he is a contemporary, a man in the street making a claim that gives offence now, today, to this reader. Christendom, the book argues, is the arrangement whereby a whole country is Christian by being born there, and therefore nobody in it is. He sends a copy to Bishop Mynster. Tradition has it that Mynster was displeased; what passed between the two men is not on record, and four more years go by without a word from either.
stops.quote: Even as a small child I was told, as solemnly as possible: that everyone spat at Christ (who, indeed, was the truth), that the multitude (those who passed by) spat at him and said: 'Shame on you.' I have kept this deep in my heart. This thought is my life.
stops.quote_source: Journals, quoted via Frithiof Brandt's commentary at sorenkierkegaard.org; no entry number or translator given there
suggested_refs: Indøvelse i Christendom (1850), by Anti-Climacus

stops.name: Vor Frue Kirke, the witness to the truth
stops.date_confidence: Mynster's death on 30 January 1854, and Martensen's eulogy as the trigger for the church attack, are attested (sorenkierkegaard.org; Wikipedia, 'Søren Kierkegaard'). The venue is [R]: the funeral is inferred to have been held at the cathedral where Mynster presided and was not independently confirmed. The date is set to February 1854, the month of the funeral, since no exact day was established.
stops.campa: Mynster dies on the thirtieth of January, and at the funeral Hans Lassen Martensen, who wants the see and will get it, calls the dead bishop a link in the chain of witnesses to the truth reaching back to the apostles. Kierkegaard hears the phrase and it detonates in him. A witness to the truth, in his vocabulary, is somebody persecuted, poor, and killed for it, not a court preacher in silk who died in his bed at eighty. He writes the article that week and puts it in a drawer, where it stays until December.
suggested_refs: H. L. Martensen's funeral address for Bishop Mynster, Copenhagen, February 1854

stops.name: Fædrelandet, the first article
stops.date_confidence: attested (sorenkierkegaard.org; Wikipedia, 'Søren Kierkegaard'). The Fædrelandet office address is [R], a reconstructed placement in central Copenhagen. Peter Christian Kierkegaard's dismay at the campaign is [R], biographical tradition, not verified against a source fetched in this pass.
stops.campa: Ten months after the funeral he prints the question and then answers it: was Bishop Mynster a witness to the truth, one of the authentic witnesses to the truth? He keeps going all winter and into the spring, article after article, against Martensen, against the thousand livings, against the arrangement by which a man is baptized into Christianity the way he is registered into a nationality. His own brother Peter Christian, an archdeacon of that church, is appalled.
stops.quote: True worship of God consists, very simply, in doing God's will.
stops.quote_source: 'The Present Moment' [Øieblikket], trans. Lee M. Hollander, Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard (1923)
suggested_refs: Kierkegaard's articles in Fædrelandet, December 1854 to May 1855

stops.name: Copenhagen, Øieblikket
stops.date_confidence: The periodical and its nine numbers in his lifetime are attested (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy); the pool gives May 1855 without a day, so the day is defaulted. The coordinate is [R], a reconstructed central Copenhagen placement: the paper was self-financed and no editorial address turned up in the sources consulted. The sentence about ceasing to take part paraphrases the argument of the issues and is not offered as a quotation.
stops.campa: From May he publishes his own paper, The Moment, at his own expense, nine numbers in seven months, sold in the street. The prose is short and loud and there are no pseudonyms left in it. He is spending the last of his father's money on the printing, and he knows the money will run out about when he does. Stop taking part, he tells the reader: whatever else your life is, by ceasing to take part in the public worship of God as it now is, you have one guilt the less, and a great one.
stops.quote: The whole ramshackle pile of a State Church which has not been aired, spiritually speaking, in times out of mind the air in it has developed a taint.
stops.quote_source: 'The Present Moment' [Øieblikket], trans. Lee M. Hollander, Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard (1923)
suggested_refs: Øieblikket, nine numbers, May to September 1855, self-published in Copenhagen

stops.name: Frederiks Hospital, the collapse
stops.date_confidence: attested (sorenkierkegaard.org; Wikipedia, 'Søren Kierkegaard'). The conversations of the last weeks are recorded by Emil Boesen himself and are the principal witness for them. Coordinate contradiction inside the pool, not resolved: the geography lens gives 55.687, 12.5936 for this building and the afterlife lens gives 55.6867, 12.5925. The geography figure is used at both hospital stops for consistency.
stops.campa: He falls in the street and is carried to Frederiks Hospital on Bredgade. The legs go first and keep going: he cannot stand, then cannot move at all below the waist, and stays entirely clear in the head the whole time. His schoolfriend Emil Boesen, now a pastor, comes to sit at the bedside and takes down what he says, day after day, in a notebook. He tells Boesen he wants to be rid of the body, and that his life was a great suffering nobody else knew about.
suggested_refs: Emil Boesen's record of the hospital conversations, October and November 1855

stops.name: Frederiks Hospital, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested (sorenkierkegaard.org; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Wikipedia). The cause of death is genuinely unresolved: the record's entry is tentative and no autopsy was performed, so tuberculosis of the spine must not be stated as settled. The Designmuseum Danmark occupancy of the remodelled building is attested (Wikipedia, 'Frederiks Hospital'). The span of the journals counts from the first surviving entry, 15 April 1834, and is arithmetic rather than a source's phrase.
stops.campa: Forty days in the hospital, and he dies there at forty-two. He has refused communion from the pastor sent to him, saying he will take it from a layman or not at all, since the clergy are civil servants of the king. The cause of death goes into the record tentatively, with a question mark, and no autopsy is performed; nobody since has settled it. He leaves an estate of almost nothing and twenty-one years of journals. The building is remodelled in the 1920s and holds the Danish museum of design now.
suggested_refs: Frederiks Hospital on Bredgade, remodelled in the 1920s as Designmuseum Danmark

stops.name: Vor Frue Kirke, the funeral
stops.date_confidence: The funeral at Vor Frue Kirke on 18 November 1855 is attested (sorenkierkegaard.org). That the congregation was largely students, and that his brother Peter Christian preached, are [R], biographical tradition not re-verified against a source fetched in this pass. Coordinate corrected as at the confirmation stop.
stops.campa: The cathedral is full and much of the crowd is students. The man who spent the last year of his life telling Denmark that its church was a fraud is buried out of that church by its clergy, at his family's arrangement, with his brother the archdeacon in the pulpit. Nobody consults the dead man's published position on the question, which is on record in nine numbers of a paper sold in this street. The service goes off without incident. The trouble starts at the grave.
suggested_refs: The funeral service at Vor Frue Kirke, 18 November 1855

stops.name: Assistens Cemetery, the nephew's protest
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Søren Kierkegaard'; sorenkierkegaard.org): Henrik Lund protested, was prosecuted for disturbing the service, and was fined. Which passages he read is [R]. Coordinate contradiction inside the pool, not resolved: the geography lens gives 55.6913, 12.5514 and the afterlife lens 55.6908, 12.5494; the geography figure is used. Correction to the pool's afterlife lens, which had Regine dying in the Danish West Indies: Wikipedia gives 18 March 1904, in Copenhagen, aged 82, buried at Assistens near Kierkegaard and Schlegel.
stops.campa: At the graveside in Nørrebro his nephew Henrik Lund, a physician, steps forward without warning and reads aloud, saying that the dead man had broken with this church and that burying him by its rites falsifies him. There is uproar. Lund is prosecuted for disturbing a funeral and fined. Kierkegaard goes into the family plot alongside the father who cursed God on a heath and the mother he never wrote a line about. Regine Schlegel will be buried in this same ground in 1904.
suggested_refs: The Kierkegaard family plot at Assistens Kirkegård, Nørrebro, and the court case against Henrik Lund

stops.name: Royal Library Garden, the statue
stops.date_confidence: The 1879 installation and Louis Hasselriis's authorship are attested (Wikipedia, 'Louis Hasselriis'); day and month defaulted, and no unveiling details or physical description of the statue turned up in the sources consulted, which is a gap. The 1889 encyclopedia phrasing and the 1861 German translation of Øieblikket are attested via Wikipedia, 'Søren Kierkegaard'.
stops.campa: Twenty-four years after the funeral, Louis Hasselriis sets a seated bronze of him in the library garden behind Christiansborg. The Moment had gone into German by 1861, and the country that was told from a self-financed paper that its church was a fraud has begun treating the man who told it as a national possession. By 1889 an encyclopedia can call him the most original thinker and theological philosopher the North ever produced, and note that his reputation has been climbing steadily since his death.
suggested_refs: Louis Hasselriis's seated Kierkegaard, Det Kongelige Biblioteks Have, Copenhagen, 1879

stops.name: Søren Kierkegaard Research Centre, the fifty-five volumes
stops.date_confidence: The SKS edition, its 55 volumes, its 1997-2013 span and its free online access are attested (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy); day and month defaulted. Two corrections to the pool: Walter Lowrie's 1941 title is Training in Christianity, not Practice in Christianity, which is the Hong title of 1991, and the Princeton Kierkegaard's Writings series is listed by the publisher as 27 volumes rather than 26, so no number is given here. Alexander Dru's 1938 first English journals is attested (Wikipedia). That the 2013 completion falls on the bicentenary is arithmetic, not a source's framing.
stops.campa: The papers he left, journals, drafts, loose sheets, are edited at the university into Søren Kierkegaards Skrifter: fifty-five volumes between 1997 and 2013, put online free for anyone. The edition finishes in the year of his two hundredth birthday. In English he had arrived earlier and unevenly: Alexander Dru's journals in 1938, Walter Lowrie's Training in Christianity in 1941, then the Hongs' Princeton series. Most of the world now reads him in the Hongs.
suggested_refs: Søren Kierkegaards Skrifter (SKS), 55 vols., Søren Kierkegaard Research Centre, University of Copenhagen, 1997-2013
Kierkegaard's Writings, gen. eds. Howard V. and Edna H. Hong, Princeton University Press
